title: Growth Paths in Early Machine Learning Ventures: Technical Configuration and Competitive Advantage Over Time
authors: Jack Fraser; Pinar Ozcan
affiliations: Imperial College Business School, Management and Entrepreneurship, London, England, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; University of Oxford, Saïd Business School, Oxford, Oxfordshire, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
abstract: Machine learning capabilities have become important strategic assets, yet little is known about how their technical characteristics affect the competitive advantage of the firms that build them. Through an inductive, multicase study tracking six early-stage machine learning ventures in an accelerator program, we explore how their phases of specialization and exploration may be constrained by properties of the underlying technology. Our findings show how training data, learning paradigms, and model outputs depend on one another and on the applications they serve, and how these relationships change over time. This interdependence shapes firms’ growth paths, alternately expanding or limiting the strategic options available to them. Characteristics that confer an early competitive advantage can constrain later growth. We discuss the implications for strategy research on competitive advantage and path dependence in machine learning ventures.

title: Bellman Optimality of Average-Reward Robust Markov Decision Processes with a Constant Gain
authors: Shengbo Wang; Nian Si
affiliations: University of Southern California, Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Los Angeles, California, United States; HKUST, IEDA, Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: Learning and optimal control under robust Markov decision processes (MDPs) have received increasing attention, yet most existing theory, algorithms, and applications focus on finite-horizon or discounted models. Long-run average-reward formulations, while natural in many operations research and management contexts, remain underexplored. This is primarily because the dynamic programming foundations are technically challenging and only partially understood, with several fundamental questions remaining open. This paper steps toward a general framework for average-reward robust MDPs by analyzing the constant-gain setting. We study the average-reward robust control problem with possible information asymmetries between the controller and an S-rectangular adversary. Our analysis centers on the constant-gain robust Bellman equation, examining both the existence of solutions and their relationship to the optimal average reward. Specifically, we identify when solutions to the robust Bellman equation characterize the optimal average reward and stationary policies, and we provide one-sided weak communication conditions ensuring solutions' existence. These findings expand the dynamic programming theory for average-reward robust MDPs and lay a foundation for robust dynamic decision making under long-run average criteria in operational environments.

title: Combinatorial Inference on the Optimal Assortment in Multinomial Logit Models
authors: Shuting Shen; Xi Chen; Ethan Xingyuan Fang; Junwei Lu
affiliations: Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States; New York University, Stern School of Business, New York, New York, United States; Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, United States
abstract: Assortment optimization has been extensively explored in recent decades due to its practical significance. Despite the substantial literature on optimization algorithms and latent score estimation, there remains a need to explore uncertainty quantification for the optimal assortment. Instead of estimating and recovering the complete optimal offer set, decision-makers may be interested in testing whether a given property holds for the optimal assortment. For instance, they may wish to determine whether certain products of interest should be included in the optimal set or ascertain how many categories of products the optimal set should contain. This paper proposes a novel inferential framework for testing such properties within the context of the widely adopted multinomial logit (MNL) model. In this model, each customer is assumed to purchase an item within the offered products with a probability proportional to the underlying preference score associated with the product. We reduce inferring a general optimal assortment property to quantifying the uncertainty associated with the sign change point detection of the marginal revenue gaps. We establish the asymptotic normality of the marginal revenue gap estimator and construct a maximum statistic using the gap estimators to detect the sign change point. By approximating the distribution of the maximum statistic through multiplier bootstrap techniques, we propose a valid testing procedure. Numerical experiments are also conducted to assess the performance of our method.

title: Uncertainty Attitudes, Subjective Beliefs, and Decisions Under Uncertainty
authors: Adeline Delavande; Jayant Ganguli; Friederike Mengel
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Technology Sydney, Ultimo, New South Wales 2007, Australia; Department of Economics, University of Essex, Colchester CO4 3SQ, United Kingdom; Department of Economics, University of Essex, Colchester CO4 3SQ, United Kingdom; and Department of Applied Economics, Erasmus University Rotterdam, Burgemeester Oudlaan 50, Rotterdam 3062 PA, Netherlands
abstract: We conducted survey experiments to gather new data on uncertainty attitudes and subjective beliefs. Our survey targets a general population, focusing on health and financial decisions. We collect data on (i) individual attitudes toward risk and ambiguity, including individual-specific probability weighting and loss aversion, and (ii) individual probabilistic beliefs about events related to the decisions we consider. The joint availability of individual preference parameters and subjective beliefs allows us to study heterogeneity and cross-correlations across these parameters in depth and to estimate structural models of decision making under uncertainty that go beyond subjective expected utility. We find that both preferences and beliefs are highly heterogeneous. Compared with subjective expected utility, prospect theory combined with source-dependent probability weighting fits the data strictly better in some contexts and equally well in others. Prospect theory performs particularly well when the belief distribution is concentrated toward extreme values. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: A. title: Recommender Systems Under Privacy Protection
authors: Can Küçükgül; Özalp Özer; Shouqiang Wang
affiliations: Rutgers School of Business, Camden, New Jersey 08102; FBA Science, Selling Partner Services, Amazon, Seattle, Washington 98109; and Naveen Jindal School of Management, The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas 75080; Naveen Jindal School of Management, The University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas 75080
abstract: We examine how a profit-driven platform designs its recommender policies under varying privacy protection regimes. We demonstrate a functional equivalence between opt-out protection and unprotected privacy. Notably, granting consumers the autonomy to misrepresent personal data can compel the platform to distort recommendations, inadvertently harming both parties. When recommendations are purely informative, such privacy controls can deter personalization entirely. However, when recommendations also serve an allocative role—controlling product access—algorithmic discrimination may emerge, restricting the disadvantaged minority from valuable opportunities. These findings remain robust even with endogenous profit margins. This paper was accepted by Omar Besbes, revenue management and market analytics. title: Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
authors: Sumit Agarwal; Pengsheng Lin; Yupeng Lin; Ruichang Lu; Xiaojun Zhang
affiliations: NUS Business School, National University of Singapore, Singapore; School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China; Guanghua School of Management, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China
abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Consistent with diagnostic expectation theory, higher exposure to Ebola fear does not result in a significant learning effect during the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal acknowledges the financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. Y. title: When Scientific Uncertainty is Linked to Lower Information Avoidance: Motivational Pathways to Public Engagement With Climate Risk Information
authors: Soo Jung Hong
affiliations: Department of Communications and New Media Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences National University of Singapore Singapore Singapore
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how scientific uncertainty is associated with both appetitive and aversive motivations, as well as its direct and indirect associations with risk information avoidance (RIA). Drawing on Liu and Chen's (2026) appetitive–aversive motivational framework, based on the Planned Risk Information Avoidance (PRIA) model, we investigate how uncertainty relates to information avoidance through risk perception, perceived information insufficiency, informational efficacy, information overload, information‐seeking norms, and negative emotions. Using structural equation modeling with a US adult sample, the findings indicate that scientific uncertainty is negatively associated with information avoidance and is linked to multiple motivational pathways. Specifically, higher scientific uncertainty is associated with greater risk perceptions and information insufficiency, and with lower levels of information overload, which in turn correspond to reduced avoidance intentions. These findings provide insight into the role of scientific uncertainty in shaping RIA, highlighting its potential to reduce avoidance in the context of climate change.

title: Public Risk Judgments of Endocrine‐Disrupting Chemicals: Psychometric Structure, Exposure Pathways, and Cross‐National Differences
authors: Nick Simonsen; Aleksandr Pravednikov; Carl‐Johan Lagerkvist; Sonja Perkovic
affiliations: Department of Management Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark; Department of Economics Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, Uppsala, Sweden
abstract: ABSTRACT Endocrine‐disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are pervasive in everyday life and pose well‐documented public health risks, yet little is known about how lay perceptions of EDC risks are structured and how they vary across exposure pathways and regulatory contexts. Drawing on the psychometric paradigm of risk perception, we conducted a large cross‐national survey () in Denmark, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Participants evaluated 18 EDC‐related exposure scenarios across nine canonical risk attributes, ranked perceived health risks by exposure pathway (consumption, inhalation, and dermal contact), and reported perceived severity, susceptibility, overall health risk, institutional trust, and sociodemographic characteristics. Across all three countries, risk perceptions exhibited a robust two‐dimensional structure corresponding to affective‐dread and cognitive‐deliberate dimensions. However, the relative salience of these dimensions varied systematically: cognitive‐deliberate cues accounted for more variance in Denmark, whereas affective‐dread cues were more prominent in the United Kingdom and the United States. Perceived risk also varied consistently by exposure pathway, with consumption judged the most risky, followed by inhalation and dermal contact, a hierarchy that showed minimal cross‐country variation. At the individual level, greater knowledge of EDCs consistently predicted higher perceived susceptibility, while gender, year of birth, income, parenthood, and institutional trust showed context‐ and outcome‐specific associations. By extending the psychometric paradigm to chronic, diffuse chemical hazards embedded in everyday activities, this study demonstrates that EDC risk perceptions reflect shared affective‐cognitive dimensions while remaining sensitive to exposure pathways and governance contexts, offering theoretically grounded insights for risk communication and policy design.

title: EXPRESS: The Implications of Generic Responses in Online Customer Service Operations
authors: Jitsama Tanlamai; Wreetabrata Kar; Warut Khern-am-nuai; Yossiri Adulyasak
abstract: Businesses use a range of strategies to manage online customer service, with social media serving as a popular platform. A growing practice in social-media customer service is the use of generic responses to address customer inquiries. Our study investigates the impact of these generic responses on customer engagement and satisfaction. We analyze social media data from one of the largest banks in the United States and apply machine-learning techniques to extract relevant information from textual data. We leverage a quasi-experimental setting in which a generic response to a customer’s inquiry serves as the treatment. We find that generic responses increase the likelihood that customers reply to the bank. Among customers who reply, generic responses are associated with lower satisfaction. However, our further analyses show that under certain conditions, strategic use of generic responses is associated with higher customer satisfaction. Our findings provide guidance to operation managers regarding how generic responses can be tailored and used to improve online customer service operations.

title: Walk the talk: how procurement professionals' interpretations shape social sustainability cascading
authors: Svetlana Castre de Chabot; Salomee Ruel; Anicia Jaegler; Stefan Gold
affiliations: KEDGE Business School Sustainability Center of Excellence, , ,; OCRE Research Lab, EDC Paris Business School , ,; De Vinci Research Center, De Vinci Higher Education , ,; Technical University of Munich TUM Campus Straubing for Biotechnology and Sustainability, , ,
abstract: Purpose Procurement professionals shape how firms translate their commitments to social sustainability into supplier-facing governance, which can vary markedly, even within the same firm. This study explains this variation by theorizing how procurement professionals interpret their role and translate engagement with suppliers into governance practices. Design/methodology/approach The study draws on constructivist grounded theory and interviews with 27 professionals across organizational contexts. The analysis combines iterative coding, constant comparison, theoretical sampling, and abductive engagement with sensitizing literature. Findings The study develops a process model that explains cascading depth from a people-centric perspective. The interviewed procurement professionals differed on whether they construed their remit to include social sustainability, whether supplier-facing action appeared worth pursuing, and whether more improvement-oriented engagement appeared feasible. This situated judgment shaped whether cascading is enacted predominantly through procedural compliance or through more generative supplier-facing practice. Prospective paradoxical sensemaking helped explain how more generative supplier-facing responses could remain actionable under competing commercial demands, as professionals saw anticipated social and commercial consequences as relevant to their judgment in the present. Originality/value The study reframes cascading depth as a matter of how procurement professionals enact governance mechanisms. It specifies interpretive and relational conditions that remain underexplored in the literature on sustainable behavioral supply chain management. It extends paradoxical sensemaking research on how tensions are framed to include how more generative responses may be established and sustained in practice.

title: Digital transformation of service ecosystems: an orchestration perspective
authors: Bingyu Han; Liangjuan Qin; Liang Li; Wei Zhang
affiliations: School of International Trade and Economics, University of International Business and Economics , ,; School of Artificial Intelligence and Data Science, University of International Business and Economics , ,; College of Management, University of Massachusetts Boston , , ,
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how digital transformation unfolds within logistics service ecosystems and how inter-actor operational connections and coordinating roles change over time from an orchestration perspective. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted a case study of three international inland ports in China. Data were triangulated through interviews, observations and documents to capture ecosystem-level orchestration practices and transformation evolution. Findings The authors developed a process model that identifies three evolutionary stages of the digital transformation of service ecosystems: developing digital connectivity, tapping digital service potential and co-creating digital value. The model demonstrates how actors employ resource and network orchestration at each stage. The analysis reveals how these two forms of orchestration interact and how orchestration dynamics change over time. Originality/value This study shifts the focus of digital transformation research from a few focal firms to service ecosystems overall. It theorizes a three-stage transformation process, reveals the evolving interplay between resource and network orchestration, shows that different actors can assume orchestration leadership, and provides actionable recommendations for managers seeking to digitally transform logistics and supply chain service ecosystems.

title: Navigating Institutional Friction in Digital Transformation: A Mechanism‐Based View
authors: Hugo Hedlund; Katrin Jonsson; Johan Sandberg
affiliations: Department of Informatics Umeå University Umeå Sweden
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital transformation (DT) fundamentally alters organizational structures, practices, and values, frequently generating significant friction as incoming digital artefacts structurally misalign with legacy institutional demands. These demands are rooted in institutional logics—the deeply held belief systems and practices that guide organizational behaviour. Drawing on a 15‐year longitudinal case study of a Swedish municipality, this study investigates how public‐sector entities manage this friction over time. The findings reveal DT as a dynamic, recursive trajectory driven by three sociotechnical mechanisms: Consolidation, Control, and Negotiation. These mechanisms generate non‐linear shifts across institutional states of conflict and alignment. This study makes three contributions. First, it reconceptualizes DT theory by framing transformation as recursive, non‐linear cycles of divergence and convergence that redirect, suppress, or accommodate localized, logic‐based resistance. Second, it advances the logic multiplicity framework by demonstrating how digital artefacts alter sociotechnical coupling, thereby shifting the centrality and compatibility of competing demands. Third, it illuminates the causal architecture of macro‐level institutional change, detailing the observable actions used to navigate logic‐based resistance during DT.

title: Differences in gender pension gaps in public and private pensions in West Germany: An analysis sensitive to interdependencies across the life course
authors: Carla Rowold
affiliations: University of Oxford, UK; Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research, Germany; Max Planck–University of Helsinki Center for Social Inequalities in Population Health, Rostock, Germany and Helsinki, Finland; Hertie School, Germany; Einstein Center Population Diversity (ECPD), Germany
abstract: Gender pension gaps (GPG) surpass gender wage gaps in most European countries. Research has largely relied on single-factor, employment-centred explanations, and we know less about how GPGs emerge from an interdependent life-course perspective. This study contributes to research on gender pension gaps and cumulative (dis)advantage across the life course by applying a life-course-sensitive decomposition to linked survey–register data for Germany (SHARE-RV), comparing gender gaps in public and private pensions based on common work–family life courses, including relative earning positions, relevant due to pension privatisation in Europe. It considers the interdependencies of employment, family life and earnings over the life course. GPGs occur because privileged life courses yielding high pensions are almost exclusively accessible to fathers, while female-typical life-course patterns characterised by care work and part-time employment yield low pensions. Gendered access to high-income careers drives the GPG in private pensions more strongly than in public pensions, underscoring the future risk of high GPGs given persistent gender wage inequalities and pension privatisation in Germany.

title:

                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Skill Acquisition and Labor Market Returns
authors: Ting Ren; Xuhang Shen
affiliations: HSBC Business School Peking University Shenzhen China
abstract: ABSTRACT Using resumes from a major Chinese online recruitment platform, we document gender gaps in reported AI skills and their labor‐market associations. Women are less likely to report AI skills. Gelbach decompositions show that major choice, occupational sorting, and complementary skills account for part of this gap, while a sizable residual remains. Reported AI skills are associated with higher wages, but the association is weaker for women. Women with AI skills also sort less into AI‐requiring jobs. Employer responses improve when applicants' reported AI skills match job requirements, with no statistically significant gender difference detected.

title: Issue‐Centric Orchestration of Climate Transition: The Case of Transition Risk Governance
authors: Niina Hakala; Fatma Jemaa
affiliations: University of Turku; EDHEC Business School
abstract: Abstract A decade ago, climate transition fell outside the mandates of financial regulators, central banks, accounting standard‐setting bodies, and financial‐market actors. Today, it is central to financial‐market governance aimed at steering business conduct toward a low‐carbon economy. Drawing on a longitudinal study of climate transition as a financial governance concern from 2010 to 2021, we show how governance authority over emerging sustainability concerns is assembled when no actor has an established mandate to address those concerns. Informed by Latour's concept of matter of concern, our analysis reveals how climate transition became constituted as transition risk, was stabilized through the private industry‐led Task Force on Climate‐related Financial Disclosures, and was translated across interconnected governance sites. We develop a three‐phase process model of issue‐centric orchestration – issue emergence, stabilization, and translation – unpacking how governance authority is progressively assembled through the trajectory of transition risk. The study contributes to public–private governance research by showing how private governance initiatives can reshape and extend, rather than displace or reduce, public authority. It further advances orchestration research by showing how interdependent governance arrangements form around shared concerns across governance domains and jurisdictions.

Making ‘Gender‐Lens Investing’ Work: Cultivating Proto‐Infrastructure for Alternative Financial Futures
authors: Danielle Logue; Markus A. Höllerer; Yi Zhao; Tanja Ohlson
affiliations: UNSW Sydney; WU Vienna; IAE Business School; Frankfurt School of Finance and Management
abstract: Abstract This study examines how elites engage in prefigurative organizing and construct the institutional infrastructure for enacting alternative futures. We investigate their engagement in gender‐lens investing (GLI) within the global movement for gender equality in finance and investment. Using fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) of 28 GLI mutual funds and exchange‐traded funds, we diagnose how fund managers combine available resources to prefigure GLI as investment products, identifying distinct configurations of symbolic, relational, and material resources through which GLI is enacted and made recognizable and actionable in the present. In doing so, we show that prefigurative efforts are not exclusive to grassroots activism, and demonstrate that the infrastructure supporting alternative practices is built through elites' efforts to recombine existing institutional resources into proto‐infrastructure. We therefore contribute a combinatorial perspective of prefigurative organizing that highlights the role of elites, and introduces proto‐infrastructure as a conceptual device for theorizing how prefigurative practices begin to acquire an incipient institutional form prior to the full consolidation of institutional infrastructure. This combinatorial perspective offers a new and timely lens for understanding GLI, impact investing, and the gender equality movement under current political backlash.

title: Leaders as Theorists
authors: Teppo Felin; Robert E. Ployhart; Todd Zenger
affiliations: University of Utah; University of Oxford; University of South Carolina
abstract: Abstract Research on leadership has long focused on two extremes, either on individual traits (or styles and behaviours) or on relationships and context. We argue that neither extreme explains where leadership originates from or how it produces the collective outcomes it is credited with. We propose a third view that is neither a compromise between nor a variant of these extremes. We argue that leaders are theorists. Leaders are forward‐looking actors who, at any level of an organization, formulate causal theories and frame problems. The value of leader theories is realized, amplified or constrained through social mechanisms. Theorizing is not one activity among many – it is the act that constitutes leading itself. The very factors foregrounded by recent work in leadership (like context, trust, and relationality) are not the starting point of leadership but emerge as leaders advocate, adopt, test, and scale theories. The leader‐as‐theorist agenda is normative and interventionist, highlighting how leader theorizing and causal reasoning can be improved and taught. We close by laying out a research agenda for studying leaders as theorists.

title:
Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    and the architecture of knowledge work: Expertise bypass, exchange governability, and shifting bottlenecks
authors: Michael G. Jacobides; Mingyu Dalbert Ma; Amartya Das; Matt Langione; Sesh Iyer
affiliations: Strategy & Entrepreneurship Area London Business School London UK; BCG Institute The Boston Consulting Group Inc Boston Massachusetts USA; Chubb Chubb Limited New York New York USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Research on GenAI and work has largely focused on tasks. We ask when task‐level effects alter knowledge‐work industry architecture: the allocation of activities across firm boundaries. Using a three‐stage abductive design—an executive roundtable, a panel of 626 firm websites (2017–2025), and 33 interviews plus two further roundtables with C‐level executives and corporate directors—we document divergent repositioning: professional services firms foreground relational value, while interface‐oriented technology firms emphasize scalable interfaces. We find that activity reallocation is shaped by two independently varying dimensions: expertise bypass and exchange governability. Their intersection yields four configurations: contestable reallocation, persistent bundles with selective insourcing, federated expert provision, and integrated expert provision. We extend industry architecture theory by explaining change when production and exchange conditions shift separately. Managerial Summary GenAI is not simply making knowledge work more efficient—it may be changing which organizations perform which work. We document that professional services firms are emphasizing relationship‐driven, judgment‐intensive work, while interface‐oriented technology firms are extending scalable delivery. Our framework explains why task exposure alone does not determine where work moves. We distinguish between expertise bypass—whether GenAI can produce an output without the expertise previously required—and exchange governability—whether that activity can be specified, verified, priced, and warranted across firm boundaries. Where both are present, work becomes contestable and may be reallocated. Where they diverge, highly exposed activities may remain bundled, while less exposed, human‐intensive work may move through federated specialist models. These conditions shape which organizational forms become viable.

title: Team diversity and radical green innovation: a patent-based analysis of gender, geographic, and institutional effects
authors: Daniel Coronado; Esther Ferrándiz; Rosario Marín; Carmen Puentes
abstract: Abstract Achieving ambitious climate goals hinges on radical green innovation, yet how inventor-team composition shapes the radicalness of green patents remains largely unexplored. Drawing on theories of knowledge heterogeneity and recombination, we jointly assess three dimensions of diversity that prior work has typically examined in isolation: gender and geographic diversity among inventors, and institutional diversity among co-assignees. We analyze 124,114 green patent families filed at the European Patent Office between 1990 and 2020 using fractional response models. Gender diversity shows a negative association with radicalness, contrasting with evidence from general, technology-wide patenting, where gender diversity has been linked to greater novelty. Geographic diversity is positively related to radicalness in the full population and remains positive among co-assigned patents, though with weaker statistical support in this smaller subsample. Institutional diversity displays a positive but modest association within the 12,267 co-assigned families for which it can be measured. Among collaboration types, partnerships with universities show a positive link, whereas inter-firm ones show a negative one. These patterns hold broadly across alternative diversity measures, estimation methods, and additional sensitivity analyses. Overall, our results demonstrate that diversity is not uniformly related to radical green innovation: its implications vary across dimensions of diversity and depend on the organizational context in which heterogeneous knowledge is integrated. These findings underscore the importance of adopting a multidimensional perspective on team diversity and offer implications for innovation management and public policies aimed at fostering radical green innovation.

title: Presidential Address: Human Finance: Incorporating Insights from the Life Sciences
authors: ULRIKE MALMENDIER
abstract: ABSTRACT Many of the key determinants of human behavior identified in the life sciences, such as stress response, impulse control, and mood regulation, remain absent from standard economic and finance models. This paper illustrates how such insights can enhance economic models in the context of inflation expectations. Combining a retrospective survey that elicits personal inflation histories with an experimental intervention that induces the reexperiencing of historic inflation, I show that physiological, emotional, and cognitive stress markers predict heightened inflation expectations and sharper memory recall, while also shaping personal economic narratives. These findings suggest novel policy tools to counter the persistent scars of economic distress and crisis experiences, for example, by designing experiences to provide predictability and control.

title: Private Firm Disclosures and Public Firms' Debt Choice
authors: Fengqin Chen; Jeffrey Pittman; Walid Saffar
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics; Memorial University; Virginia Tech; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
abstract: ABSTRACT Analyzing a cross-country sample, we provide evidence implying that private firm disclosure transparency narrows information asymmetry, which, in turn, lowers public firms' reliance on bank debt. Channel tests help substantiate that private firm disclosure elicits this positive externality, evident in lower monitoring demand, lower borrowing costs, and higher credit rating quality. Cross-sectional results suggest that the impact of private firm transparency is larger when public firms suffer worse information opacity, private firm disclosures are more important to their public peers, and bond markets are more developed. In relying on the staggered implementation of electronic business registers as a plausibly exogenous shock and a simulated disclosure scope as the instrumental variable, we continue to find that private firm disclosures reduce public firms' bank debt reliance, helping to alleviate endogeneity threats. Data Availability Statement: The data used in this study are obtained from publicly available sources identified in the paper. JEL Classifications: G32; G21; M41.

title:
The Effect of
                    <scp>Non‐US</scp>
                    Tax Authority Monitoring on Income Shifting by Affiliates of US Multinationals: Evidence From
                    <scp>EDGAR</scp>
                    Search Activity
authors: Sabrina Chi; Anh V. Persson; Terry Shevlin; Oktay Urcan
affiliations: California State University, Fullerton Fullerton California USA; University of Illinois at Urbana‐Champaign Champaign Illinois USA; University of California, Irvine Irvine California USA; University of Washington Seattle Washington USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments worldwide are concerned that multinational enterprises (MNEs) shift profits across borders to avoid taxes. While prior research shows that home‐country tax enforcement can reduce tax avoidance, far less is known about whether foreign tax authorities (FTAs) can constrain income shifting by MNE affiliates. We measure FTA monitoring using data on FTAs' downloads of US MNEs' annual reports filed with the SEC. We find that FTA monitoring is more intensive in higher‐tax‐rate countries with a larger MNE presence, consistent with those jurisdictions facing stronger incentives to monitor income shifting. More importantly, we find that monitoring by an affiliate's local tax authority does not systematically reduce income shifting by US MNE affiliates, whereas aggregate monitoring in the MNE group affects an affiliate even when its own local FTA is not observably monitoring it. This result is consistent with a spillover effect of FTA monitoring. This association is stronger when FTAs operate under information‐exchange treaties, when company disclosures are more detailed, and when enforcement capacity is greater. We also find positive associations between aggregate FTA monitoring and subsequent tax avoidance and tax settlements of US MNEs. Our findings suggest monitoring by multiple FTAs effectively combats MNE tax avoidance and have implications for how tax administrations design and coordinate monitoring efforts.
